articles.title: UAE completes Arab world's first solo space probe – and sets course for an asteroid
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 08 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03154-4The device will be launched on a joint UAE-US-built craft. Some researchers say it could be the last mission constructed with outside help.
articles.content:
Credit: Fadel Senna/AFP via Getty

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is on course to become the fourth space power to touch an asteroid, according to scientists and engineers involved in the country’s space programme. On 1 October, they announced the completion of a probe that is expected to career into the reddish rock known as Justicia in 2035.

The probe was designed and built in the UAE. It will now be shipped to the University of Colorado Boulder, where collaborators will integrate it with the main MBR Explorer spacecraft before a launch scheduled for March 2028.

The Emirates Mission to the Asteroid belt (EMA) will observe six asteroids using an array of cameras and spectrometers, which can analyse material composition remotely. It will also observe Venus and Mars, before the MBR Explorer spacecraft dispatches the tiny 10 kilogram probe to its final destination, the asteroid Justicia.

Justicia’s unusual red colour suggests that the asteroid contains materials more commonly found further out in the Solar System than its current orbit between Mars and Jupiter. If it originated in the outer reaches and migrated inwards, that makes it an ancient “traveller from the past” that could give clues as to how the Solar System formed and the origins of its water, said Elias Tsoutsanis, chief researcher for the Propulsion and Space Research Center at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi. The TII is a government-backed research agency that designed and developed the probe. Tsoutsanis was speaking at an event in the city on 1 October marking the probe’s completion.

Going solo

The asteroid mission will be the country’s second interplanetary venture, building on the success of its Hope orbiter, which reached Mars in 2021 after six years of development.

The UAE’s relatively quick ascent into the club of space-faring nations has come through a programme of hiring international partners who have helped to design and build their various spacecraft while also training Emirati researchers and engineers.

The progress on the latest mission shows the UAE’s growing independence in space science and technology, said computer scientist Najwa Aaraj, chief executive of the TII, at the 1 October event. Whereas every part of Hope was a collaboration, the UAE built the probe component of the EMA on its own. “I’m very confident that in the next mission, we don’t need Colorado,” she added. “Everything can be done end-to-end here.”

The country’s activities in the skies seem to be having an impact on the ground. Since the UAE announced its plan to send a mission to Mars in 2014, there has been a 30% rise in students enrolling in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, said Ahmad Belhoul Al Falasi, chair of the UAE Space Agency, at the event. Between 2015 and 2025, the number of UAE universities offering aerospace engineering and space-related degree programmes has roughly doubled, he later told Nature.

This achievement has broad significance for space exploration and STEM education in the UAE, demonstrating technological progress and inspiring societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: UAE completes its first solo space probe, aiming for an asteroid mission
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has been rapidly developing its space program, starting with its first Mars mission in 2021. The country has worked with international partners to learn and build spacecraft but is now moving toward more independent space projects.

**What happened** – On October 1, 2026, the UAE announced it finished building its first space probe entirely on its own. This small 10-kilogram probe will join the MBR Explorer spacecraft, which is scheduled to launch in March 2028. The mission, called the Emirates Mission to the Asteroid belt (EMA), plans to study six asteroids and send the probe to a red-colored asteroid named Justicia by 2035.

**Impact** – Justicia is interesting because its color suggests it came from the outer Solar System, making it a rare “traveller from the past.” Studying it could help scientists understand how the Solar System formed and where water on planets might have come from. The UAE’s ability to build the probe independently shows the country’s growing skill in space technology. It also encourages more students in the UAE to study science and engineering, with university programs in aerospace doubling in recent years.

**What’s next step** – The probe will be shipped to the University of Colorado Boulder, where it will be attached to the main spacecraft. After the 2028 launch, the mission will study Venus, Mars, and six asteroids before the probe heads to Justicia. The UAE plans to handle future missions entirely on its own, without outside help.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UAE has built its first solo space probe and is preparing to explore a unique asteroid, marking a big step in the country’s growing space expertise and education efforts.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les Émirats arabes unis terminent leur première sonde spatiale autonome en vue d’une mission sur un astéroïde
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les Émirats arabes unis (EAU) développent rapidement leur programme spatial, après leur première mission sur Mars en 2021. Le pays a collaboré avec des partenaires internationaux pour apprendre et construire des engins spatiaux, mais se dirige maintenant vers des projets plus autonomes.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 1er octobre 2026, les EAU ont annoncé avoir terminé la construction de leur première sonde spatiale entièrement conçue localement. Cette petite sonde de 10 kilogrammes sera intégrée au vaisseau spatial principal MBR Explorer, dont le lancement est prévu en mars 2028. La mission, appelée Mission des Émirats vers la ceinture d’astéroïdes (EMA), prévoit d’étudier six astéroïdes et d’envoyer la sonde vers un astéroïde rouge nommé Justicia d’ici 2035.

**Impact** – Justicia est intéressante car sa couleur suggère qu’elle vient des régions extérieures du Système solaire, ce qui en fait un « voyageur du passé » rare. L’étudier pourrait aider les scientifiques à mieux comprendre la formation du Système solaire et l’origine de l’eau sur les planètes. La capacité des EAU à construire la sonde de façon autonome montre leur montée en compétence en technologie spatiale. Cela encourage aussi davantage d’étudiants aux EAU à étudier les sciences et l’ingénierie, avec un doublement des formations universitaires en aérospatiale ces dernières années.

**Prochaine étape** – La sonde sera envoyée à l’Université du Colorado à Boulder, où elle sera fixée au vaisseau principal. Après le lancement en 2028, la mission étudiera Vénus, Mars et six astéroïdes avant que la sonde ne se dirige vers Justicia. Les EAU prévoient de réaliser leurs futures missions entièrement seuls, sans aide extérieure.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Les Émirats arabes unis ont construit leur première sonde spatiale autonome et se préparent à explorer un astéroïde unique, marquant une étape importante dans leur expertise spatiale et leurs efforts éducatifs.
articles.personality_title_es: Emiratos Árabes Unidos completa su primera sonda espacial independiente y apunta a un asteroide
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los Emiratos Árabes Unidos (EAU) han desarrollado rápidamente su programa espacial, comenzando con su primera misión a Marte en 2021. El país ha colaborado con socios internacionales para aprender y construir naves espaciales, pero ahora avanza hacia proyectos más independientes.

**Qué pasó** – El 1 de octubre de 2026, los EAU anunciaron que completaron la construcción de su primera sonda espacial hecha completamente por ellos mismos. Esta pequeña sonda de 10 kilogramos se unirá a la nave principal MBR Explorer, que se lanzará en marzo de 2028. La misión, llamada Misión de los Emiratos a la Cintura de Asteroides (EMA), estudiará seis asteroides y enviará la sonda al asteroide rojo llamado Justicia para el año 2035.

**Impacto** – Justicia es especial porque su color sugiere que proviene de las regiones externas del Sistema Solar, siendo un “viajero del pasado” raro. Estudiarlo puede ayudar a los científicos a entender cómo se formó el Sistema Solar y de dónde viene el agua en los planetas. La capacidad de los EAU para construir la sonda de manera independiente muestra que están mejorando en tecnología espacial. También ha inspirado a más estudiantes en los EAU a estudiar ciencias e ingeniería, y los programas universitarios en aeroespacial se han duplicado en los últimos años.

**Próximo paso** – La sonda será enviada a la Universidad de Colorado en Boulder, donde se integrará con la nave principal. Tras el lanzamiento en 2028, la misión estudiará Venus, Marte y seis asteroides antes de que la sonda viaje hacia Justicia. Los EAU planean realizar futuras misiones sin ayuda externa.

**Frase clave** – Los Emiratos Árabes Unidos han construido su primera sonda espacial independiente y se preparan para explorar un asteroide único, marcando un avance importante en su experiencia espacial y en la educación científica.

articles.title: NASA releases trove of Moon data from historic Artemis II flight
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03197-7Annotated images and more collected by the four astronauts could inform missions to the lunar surface.
articles.content:
Artemis II astronaut Jeremy Hansen captures images during the lunar flyby.Credit: NASA

Planetary scientists have fresh Moon joy to explore. On 7 October, NASA released more than 800 gigabytes of images, audio recordings, written notes and other data gathered by the Artemis II astronauts on their historic flight past the Moon in April.

An accompanying report chronicles observations made by the first human eyes to view the Moon up close since 1972, such as the astronauts’ description of the colours of the lunar surface and the flashes of light seen by the crew as micrometeorites pelted the Moon.

But the report also details some of the challenges of sending humans to explore the surface of Moon, as both the United States and China plan to do. As lighting conditions changed, the Artemis II astronauts’ perceptions of the lunar surface also changed, showing how difficult it is to assess the Moon’s terrain accurately. At times, sunlight overwhelmed the crew’s vision. Understanding such issues is important for future astronauts trying to avoid hazards such as craters and boulders as they navigate onto and across the Moon.

Far from home

Artemis II, which launched on 1 April and returned to Earth on 10 April, carried four astronauts around the Moon and back. The journey took the crew as much as 400,171 kilometres from Earth — the farthest that humans have ever travelled from their home planet. The goal was to test how well the mission’s Orion capsule could keep humans alive in deep space. But the astronauts also did some science, including more than six hours of lunar observation collectively dubbed “Moon joy”, during their 6 April flyby.

First photos from Artemis II: see stunning ‘Earthset’ and more

With today’s information release, “I’m really excited for the community to just take this and run,” says Marie Henderson, a planetary scientist at the University of Maryland Baltimore County in Baltimore, who is one of the mission's deputy lunar science leads. “A whole bunch of new eyes is just going to make a huge difference.”

The new lunar dataset adds to those gathered by multiple orbiters and flyby probes over the years, from many nations. Comparing and contrasting the Artemis II observations, made in-situ by human eyes, with those from robotic spacecraft can enrich understanding of the Moon, scientists say.

True colours

For instance, the astronauts’ descriptions of the colours of the lunar surface are valuable for providing a record of human perception, says Elisha Jhoti, a planetary scientist at the University of California, Los Angeles, who plans to work with the data. “The images we see from the Moon are not exact representations of what our eyes would see,” she says. The astronauts reported colours including brown, tan and green in various places on the Moon, including a shade like “mold growing on sandwich bread” in one spot, according to astronaut Christina Koch.

I was with Artemis II’s scientists during the Moon fly-by. Here’s what I saw

The new data also detail how astronauts’ perception of the degree of darkness in some craters varied as the spacecraft traveled past the Moon and lighting angles changed. That’s important information if future missions send astronauts to navigate in areas such as those near the Moon’s poles. “It’s going to be hard to be in those low-light conditions,” Henderson says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on NASA releasing a large, detailed dataset from the Artemis II mission, the first human lunar flyby since 1972, which provides valuable scientific insights and practical knowledge for future Moon exploration. This represents a significant advancement in human space exploration with broad implications for future missions and lunar science.
articles.personality_title: NASA shares detailed Moon data from Artemis II’s historic flyby
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In April 2026, NASA sent four astronauts on Artemis II, the first human mission to fly past the Moon since 1972. The trip tested new space technology and allowed the crew to observe the lunar surface closely.

**What happened** – On October 7, NASA released over 800 gigabytes of data collected by the Artemis II astronauts. This includes thousands of images, audio recordings, and written notes about the Moon’s surface, lighting, and conditions experienced during the flight.

**Impact** – This data is unique because it captures what humans actually saw and heard near the Moon, something robotic missions cannot fully provide. For example, astronauts described unusual colors on the Moon like brown, tan, and even green shades, which help scientists understand how the lunar surface really looks. They also noted how changing sunlight affected their ability to see details, a challenge for future explorers.

**What’s next step** – Scientists will study this rich dataset to improve future Moon missions, especially those that plan to land astronauts on the surface. Understanding how light and terrain affect visibility will help make walking on the Moon safer and more effective.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s release of Artemis II’s detailed Moon data offers new insights that will guide and improve human exploration of the lunar surface in the years ahead.
articles.personality_title_fr: La NASA partage des données détaillées de la mission historique Artemis II autour de la Lune
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En avril 2026, la NASA a envoyé quatre astronautes lors d’Artemis II, la première mission humaine à survoler la Lune depuis 1972. Ce voyage a testé une nouvelle technologie spatiale et permis à l’équipage d’observer de près la surface lunaire.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 7 octobre, la NASA a publié plus de 800 gigaoctets de données recueillies par les astronautes d’Artemis II. Cela comprend des milliers d’images, des enregistrements audio et des notes écrites sur la surface, l’éclairage et les conditions rencontrées pendant le vol.

**Impact** – Ces données sont uniques car elles montrent ce que les humains ont vraiment vu et entendu près de la Lune, ce que les missions robotiques ne peuvent pas totalement fournir. Par exemple, les astronautes ont décrit des couleurs inhabituelles sur la Lune comme le marron, le beige et même des teintes vertes, ce qui aide les scientifiques à mieux comprendre l’apparence réelle du sol lunaire. Ils ont aussi noté comment la lumière changeante affectait leur vision, un défi pour les futurs explorateurs.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont étudier ce riche ensemble de données pour améliorer les futures missions lunaires, notamment celles qui prévoient d’envoyer des astronautes marcher sur la surface. Comprendre comment la lumière et le terrain influencent la visibilité aidera à rendre les déplacements sur la Lune plus sûrs et efficaces.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – La publication par la NASA des données détaillées d’Artemis II offre de nouvelles connaissances pour guider et améliorer l’exploration humaine de la surface lunaire dans les années à venir.
articles.personality_title_es: La NASA comparte datos detallados de la histórica misión Artemis II alrededor de la Luna
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En abril de 2026, la NASA envió a cuatro astronautas en Artemis II, la primera misión humana que sobrevoló la Luna desde 1972. El viaje probó nueva tecnología espacial y permitió al equipo observar de cerca la superficie lunar.

**Qué pasó** – El 7 de octubre, la NASA publicó más de 800 gigabytes de datos recogidos por los astronautas de Artemis II. Esto incluye miles de imágenes, grabaciones de audio y notas escritas sobre la superficie lunar, la luz y las condiciones durante el vuelo.

**Impacto** – Estos datos son únicos porque muestran lo que los humanos realmente vieron y escucharon cerca de la Luna, algo que las misiones robóticas no pueden ofrecer completamente. Por ejemplo, los astronautas describieron colores inusuales en la Luna como marrón, beige e incluso tonos verdes, lo que ayuda a los científicos a entender mejor cómo es realmente la superficie lunar. También notaron cómo la luz cambiante afectaba su visión, un reto para futuros exploradores.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos estudiarán esta rica colección de datos para mejorar futuras misiones lunares, especialmente aquellas que planean enviar astronautas a caminar sobre la superficie. Comprender cómo la luz y el terreno afectan la visibilidad ayudará a hacer que caminar en la Luna sea más seguro y efectivo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La publicación de los datos detallados de Artemis II por parte de la NASA ofrece nuevas ideas que guiarán y mejorarán la exploración humana de la superficie lunar en los próximos años.
